results.summary_before: This project implements a Turing machine with a configurable state transition table on a single Tiny Tapeout tile. It supports manual and automatic modes, tape initialization, wrap and loop options, and bank selection, with status and tape contents shown on external LED and 7-segment displays. Control is via DIP switches and pushbuttons for clock and reset, allowing step-by-step configuration and execution. The design is intended as an educational demonstration of Turing machine operation and requires external LED PMODs, a 7-segment display, and switches for full use.

results.summary_before: This design is an 8-bit counter intended to behave like a TI CD4022B decade counter with eight outputs. It is driven by an external clock signal and an enable input, although the documentation notes that the enable does not actually work and the counter is always enabled. Testing requires a microcontroller such as an Arduino or ESP32 to generate the clock, and the outputs can drive the segments of a 7-segment LED display. The project is a first chip made in Wokwi and is documented only briefly, with the known enable bug being the main limitation.

results.summary_before: This mixed-signal design is an 8-phase buck converter controller with integrated bias and reference generation, including an ultra-low-power bandgap. It manages startup sequencing, soft-start, phase rotation, and digital configuration through a digital block, while analog blocks implement the regulation loop and generate control signals. The design includes level shifters and interfaces such as an SPI-like serial interface for configuration. Testing requires verifying both digital sequencing and analog control interactions, but the documentation provides no measured results or detailed test setup.

results.summary_before: This Verilog design is a 2-digit countdown timer that counts down in minutes from a user-set value. It uses a 100 kHz clock, and after the switch is flipped, it decrements the display every 6,000,000 ticks (one minute) until reaching zero. The design drives a multiplexed 7-segment display and includes inputs for a button and switch to set the time. It can be tested in the Wokwi simulation, and requires external hardware such as a common-cathode 7-segment display, a button, and a switch.
